questions.text: What is the primary purpose of the VACUUM command?

answers.text: Free the space occupied by dead tuples
Rebuild all indexes in the database
Create a backup copy of the table
Change the isolation level of the current transaction

questions.explanation: VACUUM processes dead row versions and frees the space they occupy for future reuse.

questions.text: Which statements about how VACUUM selects objects are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Without a table list, VACUUM processes tables in the current database that are accessible to the current user
One or more tables can be specified explicitly for vacuuming
VACUUM without a table name automatically processes every database in the cluster
When a table is specified, VACUUM must also vacuum every other table in the same schema

questions.explanation: Without an object list, VACUUM works with suitable objects in the current database; when tables are specified, it is limited to them.

questions.text: What does VACUUM ANALYZE do?

answers.text: First vacuums, then collects statistics
Only collects statistics
Only rebuilds indexes
Completely rewrites the table physically

questions.explanation: VACUUM ANALYZE combines two operations: vacuuming followed by analysis.

questions.text: What happens after a regular VACUUM without FULL? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Freed space becomes available for reuse by the same table
The physical file size usually does not decrease
The operation can normally run concurrently with ordinary reads and writes
The entire table is always rewritten into a new file

questions.explanation: Regular VACUUM frees space inside the relation for reuse but, in most cases, does not return that space to the operating system.

questions.text: What fundamentally distinguishes VACUUM FULL from regular VACUUM?

answers.text: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and can return unused space to the operating system
VACUUM FULL only updates planner statistics
VACUUM FULL does not work with table contents
VACUUM FULL only rebuilds individual indexes

questions.explanation: VACUUM FULL physically rewrites the table contents, eliminating excess free space.

questions.text: Which characteristics of VACUUM FULL must be taken into account? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It requests an exclusive lock on the table
It is substantially heavier than regular VACUUM
Rewriting the table requires additional disk space
It is intended to be run after every UPDATE

questions.explanation: A full vacuum rewrites the object, requires extra space, and takes a strong lock, so it is not intended for ordinary routine maintenance.

questions.text: Can VACUUM be executed inside a transaction block?

answers.text: No
Yes, always
Only after SAVEPOINT
Only at Serializable isolation level

questions.explanation: The VACUUM documentation explicitly states that the command cannot be executed inside a transaction block.

questions.text: Which commands can be used to perform maintenance manually? Select all that apply.

answers.text: VACUUM — perform vacuuming
ANALYZE — perform analysis
VACUUM ANALYZE — vacuum and analyze
CHECKPOINT ANALYZE — vacuum and analyze

questions.explanation: The lecture separately maps the VACUUM, ANALYZE, and VACUUM ANALYZE commands to their maintenance tasks.

questions.text: What is ANALYZE used for?

answers.text: To collect statistics about table contents for use by the query planner
To physically shrink table files
To repair damaged indexes
To drop a database

questions.explanation: ANALYZE collects statistics that the planner uses to estimate possible query plans.

questions.text: Which statements about ANALYZE are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Statistics results are stored in the pg_statistic system catalog
Analysis can be limited to explicitly specified tables
Statistics collection can be limited to specified columns
ANALYZE always rewrites the entire table

questions.explanation: ANALYZE can work with the whole accessible database, selected tables, or even selected columns, and stores planner statistics.

questions.text: In this topic, what is meant by bloat?

answers.text: Excessive physical size of tables or indexes compared with the space occupied by useful data
An increase in the number of server connections
Growth in the number of databases in the cluster
An increase in work_mem

questions.explanation: The bloat section describes a situation where tables and indexes occupy more physical space than current useful data requires.

questions.text: Which factors can cause table and index bloat? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Poor autovacuum configuration
Large-scale data changes
Long-running transactions
The mere presence of a primary key

questions.explanation: The bloat slide explicitly lists autovacuum configuration, large-scale data changes, and long-running transactions.

questions.text: What does the query from the PostgreSQL Wiki page “Show database bloat” show?

answers.text: An estimate of table and index bloat
An exact list of active transactions
The history of postgresql.conf changes
WAL contents

questions.explanation: The query shown on that page is intended to estimate table and index bloat.

source.locator: Bloat queries and Query from check_postgres

questions.text: Which consequences can table and index bloat have? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Excessive disk-space usage
Larger backups
Slower sequential scans of large tables
Less efficient index access
Automatic removal of all indexes

questions.explanation: Bloated files use more space and increase the amount of data that must be processed and stored.

questions.text: Which pgstattuple extension function returns the physical relation length, counts of live and dead tuples, and free-space volume?

answers.text: pgstattuple
pg_relation_filepath
pg_reload_conf
pg_backend_pid

questions.explanation: pgstattuple returns detailed relation statistics, including sizes of live and dead tuples and free space.

questions.text: Which metrics are present in the result of pgstattuple? Select all that apply.

answers.text: dead_tuple_count
dead_tuple_percent
free_space
free_percent
active_session_count

questions.explanation: pgstattuple provides metrics for live and dead tuples as well as free space in the relation.

questions.text: How does pgstattuple_approx differ from pgstattuple?

answers.text: It tries to avoid a full scan and estimates some metrics approximately
It always rebuilds the table before measuring it
It works only with system catalogs
It is intended exclusively for changing fillfactor

questions.explanation: pgstattuple performs a full scan, whereas pgstattuple_approx uses a cheaper approach and estimates some characteristics approximately.

questions.text: When is REINDEX an appropriate operation? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The index is corrupted
The index is heavily bloated
An index storage parameter was changed and the new value must be fully applied
Column statistics need to be collected

questions.explanation: REINDEX recreates index contents and is used, among other cases, for corruption, bloat, and fully applying changed storage parameters.

questions.text: Which form of REINDEX rebuilds all indexes of a specified table?

answers.text: REINDEX TABLE
REINDEX COLUMN
REINDEX VACUUM
ANALYZE INDEX

questions.explanation: REINDEX TABLE rebuilds every index of the specified table.

questions.text: What is true about regular REINDEX and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Regular REINDEX blocks writes to the table while rebuilding
REINDEX CONCURRENTLY allows normal write operations to continue
A nonblocking rebuild performs more work and usually takes longer
REINDEX CONCURRENTLY is guaranteed to be faster than regular REINDEX

questions.explanation: CONCURRENTLY reduces lock impact on the workload at the cost of extra passes and a longer operation.

questions.text: Which tool is intended to remove table and index bloat while minimizing long exclusive locks?

answers.text: pg_repack
initdb
pg_ctl
pg_checksums

questions.explanation: pg_repack is intended to reorganize tables and indexes while doing most of the work without holding a long exclusive lock on the table being processed.

questions.text: Which statements about pg_repack are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It is a third-party PostgreSQL extension
It can remove table and index bloat
It allows reorganization on a live system with minimal locking
It is a mandatory part of the PostgreSQL core

questions.explanation: The lecture presents pg_repack as a third-party alternative when a long exclusive lock is undesirable; the project describes itself as an extension for online table and index reorganization.

questions.text: After a large DELETE, regular VACUUM completed successfully, but the table file barely shrank. Why can this happen?

answers.text: Freed space remains inside the file and can be reused for new data
VACUUM does not process deleted row versions
The server must always be restarted after VACUUM
A table can physically shrink only after ANALYZE

questions.explanation: Regular vacuuming creates free space inside pages for reuse, but that does not imply a smaller file from the operating system's point of view.

questions.text: Which tools can be used to compare the physical sizes of a table and its indexes before and after maintenance operations? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: pg_table_size(table_name)
pg_indexes_size(table_name)
pg_backend_pid()
current_user

questions.explanation: The practical exercise suggests measuring the table size with pg_table_size and the total size of its indexes with pg_indexes_size.

questions.text: Which statements about the visibility map are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It marks pages where all row versions are visible to all snapshots
It helps VACUUM skip pages that cannot contain dead row versions
It can speed up index-only access by avoiding a table-page read for a visibility check
It exists for both tables and indexes

questions.explanation: The visibility map is stored for tables. VACUUM marks pages where all row versions are visible to all snapshots; this allows vacuuming to skip such pages and helps index-only access avoid reading the table.

questions.text: Which statements about the free space map are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It stores information about free space inside pages
It is used when inserting new row versions to find a suitable page
It can exist for both tables and indexes
It stores the commit/rollback status of each transaction

questions.explanation: The free space map reflects available space in pages and helps quickly find a page for new data. Unlike the visibility map, an FSM can exist for both tables and indexes.

source.locator: Slide 5 — Updating the free space map

questions.text: Why does PostgreSQL freeze old row versions? Select all that apply.

answers.text: So old row versions no longer depend on the specific transaction number that created them
To avoid an emergency caused by exhaustion of the 32-bit XID space
So frozen row versions are considered visible to all snapshots
To physically shrink the table file as much as possible

questions.explanation: The normal XID space is limited. Sufficiently old row versions are marked frozen: their old XID is no longer needed for visibility checks and the versions are treated as visible to all snapshots. Timely freezing prevents transaction ID wraparound.

questions.text: Which statements about autovacuum are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The autovacuum launcher schedules maintenance and starts worker processes
An autovacuum worker processes tables in one database that require maintenance
The more actively a table changes, the more frequently autovacuum may process it
Autovacuum works independently of the track_counts setting

questions.explanation: The material describes a continuously running autovacuum launcher and parallel autovacuum workers that it starts. Processing frequency depends on change activity; automatic vacuuming does not work if either autovacuum or track_counts is disabled.

source.locator: Slide 8 — Autovacuum launcher and autovacuum worker
